lesson_title: Carbon Has Four Hands: Organic Naming Decoded
hook_text: Butan-2-ol isn't a chemical name. It's a home address — and you can already read it.
clip_script: Every organic name in matric chemistry is secretly a home address, and you read it backwards. The end of the name is the family surname: A-N-E means the alkanes, plain and simple. A-N-O-L means the alcohols — the family carrying an O-H group. A-N-O-I-C acid? That's the vinegar family, the carboxylic acids. The middle of the name counts the street: meth is one carbon, eth is two, prop is three, but is four. And the numbers? House numbers. So butan-2-ol is a four-carbon street, alcohol family, with the O-H living at number two. That's it — you just read organic chemistry. Building the molecule is three passes: lay the carbon spine, attach the group at its number, fill every spare bond with hydrogen. Then the trick that catches almost every mistake in the country: count to four on every carbon. Carbon has exactly four hands — four bonds, never five, never three. Find a carbon holding five things and you've found your error before the marker does. Surname, street, house number, four hands. The biggest topic in Paper 2 runs on four moves you now know.
visual_style: A street sign morphing out of a chemical name: the suffix becomes a family crest on a gate, carbon atoms line up as numbered houses, and a cartoon carbon with four hands high-fives its neighbours.
mood: Light and empowering — a secret code cracked in sixty seconds.
pacing: Three quick reveals for the three name parts, steady build sequence, punchy four-hands finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any structure in the paper like an address book.
